title: Union-Find / Disjoint Set
tagline: Near-O(1) connectivity queries via union by rank and path compression — the engine behind Kruskal's MST algorithm.

sections.content:
The **Union-Find** (also called **Disjoint Set Union**, or DSU) data structure answers one question with remarkable efficiency: **are two elements in the same group?** It maintains a collection of disjoint sets and supports two core operations — `union(a, b)` to merge the sets containing a and b, and `find(x)` to return the canonical **representative** (root) of the set containing x. If `find(a) === find(b)`, the two elements are connected.

With two optimisations — **union by rank** and **path compression** — both operations achieve near-constant amortised time: **O(α(n))** where α is the inverse Ackermann function, which grows so slowly it is effectively O(1) for any realistic input size. This makes Union-Find the go-to structure for connectivity problems: cycle detection in graphs, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, network connectivity, and image segmentation.

sections.caption: Two disjoint sets: {0,1,2,3} with root 0, and {4,5,6} with root 4. find(3)=0, find(6)=4 — different roots means no connection.

sections.title: Social Clubs with Representatives
sections.content:
Imagine a town where every person belongs to exactly one social club. Each club has a **representative** — the person you call to confirm membership. Initially every person is their own club (n clubs, 1 member each).

**Union** is a club merger: when two clubs merge, one representative steps down and defers to the other. **Find** asks "who is your representative?" — you ask your direct contact, who asks theirs, tracing the chain upward until you reach the top. **Path compression** is a shortcut: after you find the representative, every person along the chain updates their contact directly to the top — so the next query is instant. **Union by rank** ensures that smaller clubs are always absorbed into larger ones, keeping chains short. Together, these tricks mean that no matter how many mergers happen, finding a representative takes near-constant time.

The basic implementation stores a `parent` array where `parent[i]` is the parent of element i. Initially `parent[i] = i` — each element is its own root. `find(x)` recursively follows parents until `parent[x] === x`.

**Path compression** (also called "path halving") flattens the tree during `find`: after reaching the root, every node on the path is pointed directly to the root. This amortises future finds to O(1).

**Union by rank** maintains a `rank` array (an upper bound on tree height). When merging two trees, the root with the **lower rank** is made a child of the root with the **higher rank**. If ranks are equal, either can be the parent and the winner's rank increments by 1. This keeps trees shallow — height is at most O(log n) without path compression, but with path compression the effective depth approaches constant.

**Combined complexity**: O(α(n)) per operation, where α(n) ≤ 4 for all n < 10^600. For practical purposes this is O(1).

Union-Find cannot answer questions like "what path connects a and b?" or "what are all members of a's set?" efficiently — it only answers the yes/no connectivity question. For those richer queries a graph BFS/DFS is more appropriate. The power of Union-Find is its extreme speed at the single question it is designed for.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Path compression in `find` is a one-liner: set `parent[x]` to the result of the recursive call before returning it — the recursive unwinding points every node on the path directly to the root. `union` returns `false` when the elements are already connected, which is exactly the cycle-detection signal in Kruskal's algorithm.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: Kruskal's greedy strategy adds the cheapest edge that doesn't create a cycle. Union-Find's `connected` check is the cycle oracle. Without Union-Find, detecting cycles would require BFS/DFS per edge — O(E × V) total. With Union-Find the E union-find operations cost O(E α(V)), and sorting dominates at O(E log E).

sections.content: **When an interview asks about connectivity, components, or cycle detection in an undirected graph — Union-Find is usually the cleanest solution.** The `union` return value is itself useful: it returns `false` when two nodes are already in the same set, which directly signals a cycle. For directed graph cycle detection, use DFS with a three-colour mark instead — Union-Find does not distinguish edge direction.

items: Union-Find maintains disjoint sets and answers `connected(a, b)` in near-O(1) amortised time with path compression and union by rank.
Path compression flattens the tree during find — subsequent finds on the same path are O(1).
Union by rank always attaches the shallower tree under the taller one, bounding tree height at O(log n) before compression.
Combined complexity is O(α(n)) per operation — effectively O(1) for all practical n.
Key applications: cycle detection in undirected graphs, Kruskal's MST, counting connected components, network connectivity checks, and percolation simulations.

quiz.question: What does `find(x)` return in a Union-Find structure?
options: The index of x in the parent array
The root (representative) of the set containing x
The rank of x
The size of the set containing x
quiz.explanation: find(x) traverses the parent chain from x until it reaches a node that is its own parent (the root). That root is the canonical representative of the set. Two elements are in the same set if and only if they have the same root.

quiz.question: What does path compression do during `find`?
options: Sorts the elements within a set by value
Points every node on the traversal path directly to the root
Splits large sets into smaller balanced trees
Removes the node from its current set and creates a new singleton
quiz.explanation: After find(x) locates the root, it sets parent[x] to the root, and recursively sets every ancestor on the path to point directly to the root. This flattens the tree so future find calls on those nodes are O(1).

quiz.question: What does the `rank` represent in union by rank?
options: The exact number of elements in the set
An upper bound on the height of the subtree rooted at that node
The order in which the element was inserted
The weight assigned to the element
quiz.explanation: Rank is an upper bound on tree height (it becomes inaccurate after path compression but remains a useful guide). By attaching the lower-rank tree under the higher-rank root, union by rank ensures tree height stays bounded at O(log n).

quiz.question: How does Union-Find detect a cycle when building a graph edge by edge?
options: By counting the number of union operations performed
By checking whether both endpoints of a new edge are already in the same set
By running DFS after every edge insertion
By comparing the ranks of the two endpoint nodes
quiz.explanation: Before adding edge (u, v), call find(u) and find(v). If they return the same root, u and v are already connected — adding this edge would create a cycle. This is the exact check Kruskal's algorithm uses to build an MST.

quiz.question: What is the amortised time complexity per operation with both path compression and union by rank?
options: O(1) exact
O(log n)
O(α(n)) — inverse Ackermann, effectively O(1)
O(n)
quiz.explanation: The inverse Ackermann function α(n) grows so slowly that α(n) ≤ 4 for any n less than 10^600. In practice this is treated as O(1). Neither optimisation alone achieves this — both are required together.

quiz.question: When is Union-Find NOT the right tool for a graph problem?
options: When you need to check if two nodes are in the same connected component
When you need to find the shortest path between two nodes
When you need to detect cycles in an undirected graph
When you need to count connected components
quiz.explanation: Union-Find only answers yes/no connectivity. It does not store paths or edge sequences. Shortest path requires BFS (unweighted) or Dijkstra (weighted), which maintain the actual path structure.

quiz.question: What happens to the component count when union(a, b) is called and a and b are already in the same set?
options: It decrements by 1
It increments by 1 to reflect the new edge
It stays the same — no merge occurs
It resets to n
quiz.explanation: If find(a) === find(b), the elements are already in the same component. No merge is needed — the component count is unchanged. A good implementation returns false in this case, which doubles as a cycle-detection signal.

quiz.question: In Kruskal's MST algorithm, why is Union-Find used instead of plain graph BFS?
options: BFS cannot handle weighted edges
Union-Find cycle checks are near-O(1) per edge vs O(V) per BFS — reducing MST construction from O(EV) to O(E log E)
BFS does not work on undirected graphs
Union-Find guarantees the minimum spanning tree is unique
quiz.explanation: Kruskal processes every edge once after sorting. Without Union-Find, checking whether adding an edge creates a cycle requires a BFS/DFS — O(V) per edge, O(EV) total. Union-Find reduces each check to O(α(V)), making the total O(E log E) dominated by sorting.

quiz.question: Can Union-Find detect cycles in a **directed** graph?
options: Yes, it works identically to undirected graphs
No — Union-Find is undirected; directed cycle detection needs DFS with a recursion-stack or colour marking
Yes, but only if you union in topological order
No — it can only detect self-loops
quiz.explanation: Union-Find treats every edge as undirected. In a directed graph, A→B→C→A is a cycle but Union-Find would also flag A–B–C–A in the undirected sense. For directed cycles you need DFS with a GRAY (in-stack) colour to detect back edges.

quiz.question: After n-1 successful union operations on n elements, what does the component count equal?
options: n
1 — all elements are now in a single connected component
quiz.explanation: Starting with n components (each element its own set), each successful union reduces the count by exactly 1. After n-1 merges the count reaches 1 — all elements are in one set. This is exactly the state of a spanning tree connecting all n vertices.
